issues.legal_issue: A decree declaring title to money or property is not a decree for money or other property for the purpose of value-based court fees.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations of ownership of property and sought to have an earlier decree declaring another person's ownership adjudged ineffective.
The plaintiff sought no order for recovery of money or property.
The property was valued in the plaint, but the relief claimed was declaratory.
issues.conclusion: The challenged decree was not a decree for money or other property within the meaning of Section 7(iv-A), so the value-based court fee under that provision did not apply to the declaratory claim.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as enacted by the U.P. Legislature, a 'decree for money or other property' means a decree for recovery of money or property, not a decree concerning title to it. The Court read 'for' consistently with its use elsewhere in Section 7, where it denotes obtaining a decree ordering payment or recovery. The declaratory claim was prima facie of the description in Schedule II, clause 17(iii). No earlier cases were cited.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_prior_decree: A party brought a civil suit seeking to challenge the effect of an earlier decree.
predicates.challenged_decree_declares_title: The earlier decree declared a person's title to money or property.
predicates.relief_seeks_no_recovery: The claimant sought a declaration of title without seeking an order for recovery of money or property.
predicates.declaratory_title_decree_is_not_decree_f: A decree declaring title is not treated as a decree ordering recovery of money or property.

issues.definition: When a civil suit challenges a decree that declares title and seeks no recovery, the resulting declaratory decree is not treated as a decree for recovery of property.

issues.legal_issue: A court decree is not an instrument securing money or property merely because it records an adjudication of rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought to have an earlier decree adjudged void or ineffective as against his claimed rights in property.
The earlier decree was passed ex parte and was a formal adjudication by the court, not a consent decree recording a contract between the parties.
issues.conclusion: The earlier decree was not an instrument securing money or other property within the meaning of Section 7(iv-A).
issues.legal_principle: Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as enacted by the U.P. Legislature, applies to an instrument securing money or other property having market value. A decree made after adjudication is a record of the court's formal determination of a claimed right and does not by its own force secure money or property. A consent decree may be regarded as such an instrument where it records a contract that secures money or property, because the court's seal is superadded to the parties' contract. No earlier cases were cited.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_prior_decree: A party brought a civil suit seeking to challenge the effect of an earlier decree.
predicates.prior_decree_is_adjudication: The earlier decree records a court's formal adjudication of a claimed right.
predicates.prior_decree_is_not_consent_contract: The earlier decree does not record a contract between the parties that secures money or property.
predicates.prior_decree_is_not_instrument_securing_: The earlier decree is not treated as an instrument securing money or property.

issues.definition: When a suit challenges a decree that records an adjudication rather than a property-securing consent contract, the decree is not treated as an instrument securing property.

issues.legal_issue: A claim for a declaration of title is not a subterfuge to obtain property where the property is held by another authority and the declaration would enable recognition of the claimant's rights.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought declarations of ownership of property and did not seek a direct order for delivery of it.
The District Magistrate was in possession of the disputed property.
A declaration of the plaintiff's title would enable him to seek recognition of his rights from the authority in possession.
issues.conclusion: The declaratory relief was not a device or subterfuge concealing a claim for the property, and the court fee paid on the plaint was proper.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding whether the declaratory relief was a device concealing a claim for property, the Court considered that the property was in the possession of the District Magistrate and that a declaration of title would enable recognition of the plaintiff's rights. In the context of Section 7(iv-A) of the Court Fees Act, 1870, as enacted by the U.P. Legislature, a genuine claim for a declaration of title is not converted into a claim for recovery merely because recognition of the title may follow. No earlier cases were cited.

predicates.civil_suit_seeks_declaration_of_title: A claimant brought a civil suit seeking a declaration of title to property.
predicates.property_is_held_by_another_authority: An authority other than the claimant held possession of the disputed property.
predicates.declaration_would_enable_recognition_of_: A declaration of the claimant's title would enable the claimant to obtain recognition of those rights from the authority holding the property.
predicates.declaratory_claim_is_not_subterfuge_for_: The claim for a declaration of title is not treated as a concealed claim for recovery of the property.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks a declaration of title to property held by another authority and the declaration would enable recognition of the claimant's rights, the declaratory claim is not treated as a subterfuge for recovery.
